sentences.text: Others, such as the majority of the parenchyma cells in potato tubers and the seed cotyledons of legumes, have a storage function.

sentences.heading: Plant cell > Types of plant cells and tissues > Collenchyma
sentences.text: Collenchyma cells are alive at maturity and have thickened cellulose cell walls.

sentences.heading: Plant cell > Types of plant cells and tissues > Collenchyma
sentences.text: These cells mature from meristem derivatives that initially resemble parenchyma, but differences quickly become apparent.

sentences.heading: Plant cell > Types of plant cells and tissues > Collenchyma
sentences.text: Plastids do not develop, and the secretory apparatus (ER and Golgi) proliferates to secrete additional primary wall.

sentences.heading: Plant cell > Types of plant cells and tissues > Collenchyma
sentences.text: The wall is most commonly thickest at the corners, where three or more cells come in contact, and thinnest where only two cells come in contact, though other arrangements of the wall thickening are possible.

sentences.heading: Plant cell > Types of plant cells and tissues > Collenchyma
sentences.text: Pectin and hemicellulose are the dominant constituents of collenchyma cell walls of dicotyledon angiosperms, which may contain as little as 20% of cellulose in Petasites.

sentences.heading: Plant cell > Types of plant cells and tissues > Collenchyma
sentences.text: Collenchyma cells are typically quite elongated, and may divide transversely to give a septate appearance.

sentences.heading: Plant cell > Types of plant cells and tissues > Collenchyma
sentences.text: The role of this cell type is to support the plant in axes still growing in length, and to confer flexibility and tensile strength on tissues.

sentences.heading: Plant cell > Types of plant cells and tissues > Collenchyma
sentences.text: The primary wall lacks lignin that would make it tough and rigid, so this cell type provides what could be called plastic support – support that can hold a young stem or petiole into the air, but in cells that can be stretched as the cells around them elongate.

sentences.heading: Plant cell > Types of plant cells and tissues > Collenchyma
sentences.text: Stretchable support (without elastic snap-back) is a good way to describe what collenchyma does.

sentences.heading: Plant cell > Types of plant cells and tissues > Collenchyma
sentences.text: Parts of the strings in celery are collenchyma.

sentences.heading: Plant cell > Types of plant cells and tissues > Sclerenchyma
sentences.text: Sclerenchyma is a tissue composed of two types of cells, sclereids and fibres that have thickened, lignified secondary walls laid down inside of the primary cell wall.

sentences.heading: Plant cell > Types of plant cells and tissues > Sclerenchyma
sentences.text: The secondary walls harden the cells and make them impermeable to water.

sentences.heading: Plant cell > Types of plant cells and tissues > Sclerenchyma
sentences.text: Consequently, sclereids and fibres are typically dead at functional maturity, and the cytoplasm is missing, leaving an empty central cavity.

sentences.heading: Plant cell > Types of plant cells and tissues > Sclerenchyma
sentences.text: Sclereids or stone cells, (from the Greek skleros, hard) are hard, tough cells that give leaves or fruits a gritty texture.

sentences.heading: Plant cell > Types of plant cells and tissues > Sclerenchyma
sentences.text: They may discourage herbivory by damaging digestive passages in small insect larval stages.

sentences.heading: Plant cell > Types of plant cells and tissues > Sclerenchyma
sentences.text: Sclereids form the hard pit wall of peaches and many other fruits, providing physical protection to the developing kernel.

sentences.heading: Plant cell > Types of plant cells and tissues > Sclerenchyma
sentences.text: Fibres are elongated cells with lignified secondary walls that provide load-bearing support and tensile strength to the leaves and stems of herbaceous plants.

sentences.heading: Plant cell > Types of plant cells and tissues > Sclerenchyma
sentences.text: Sclerenchyma fibres are not involved in conduction, either of water and nutrients (as in the xylem) or of carbon compounds (as in the phloem), but it is likely that they evolved as modifications of xylem and phloem initials in early land plants.

sentences.heading: Plant cell > Types of plant cells and tissues > Xylem
sentences.text: Xylem is a complex vascular tissue composed of water-conducting tracheids or vessel elements, together with fibres and parenchyma cells.

sentences.heading: Plant cell > Types of plant cells and tissues > Xylem
sentences.text: Tracheids are elongated cells with lignified secondary thickening of the cell walls, specialised for conduction of water, and first appeared in plants during their transition to land in the Silurian period more than 425 million years ago (see Cooksonia).

sentences.heading: Plant cell > Types of plant cells and tissues > Xylem
sentences.text: The possession of xylem tracheids defines the vascular plants or Tracheophytes.

sentences.heading: Plant cell > Types of plant cells and tissues > Xylem
sentences.text: Tracheids are pointed, elongated xylem cells, the simplest of which have continuous primary cell walls and lignified secondary wall thickenings in the form of rings, hoops, or reticulate networks.

sentences.heading: Plant cell > Types of plant cells and tissues > Xylem
sentences.text: More complex tracheids with valve-like perforations called bordered pits characterise the gymnosperms.

sentences.heading: Plant cell > Types of plant cells and tissues > Xylem
sentences.text: The ferns and other pteridophytes and the gymnosperms have only xylem tracheids, while the flowering plants also have xylem vessels.

sentences.heading: Plant cell > Types of plant cells and tissues > Xylem
sentences.text: Vessel elements are hollow xylem cells without end walls that are aligned end-to-end so as to form long continuous tubes.

sentences.heading: Plant cell > Types of plant cells and tissues > Xylem
sentences.text: The bryophytes lack true xylem tissue, but their sporophytes have a water-conducting tissue known as the hydrome that is composed of elongated cells of simpler construction.

sentences.heading: Plant cell > Types of plant cells and tissues > Phloem
sentences.text: Phloem is a specialised tissue for food transport in higher plants, mainly transporting sucrose along pressure gradients generated by osmosis, a process called translocation.

sentences.heading: Plant cell > Types of plant cells and tissues > Phloem
sentences.text: Phloem is a complex tissue, consisting of two main cell types, the sieve tubes and the intimately associated companion cells, together with parenchyma cells, phloem fibres and sclereids.

sentences.heading: Plant cell > Types of plant cells and tissues > Phloem
sentences.text: Sieve tubes are joined end-to-end with perforated end-plates between known as sieve plates, which allow transport of photosynthate between the sieve elements.

sentences.heading: Plant cell > Types of plant cells and tissues > Phloem
sentences.text: The sieve tube elements lack nuclei and ribosomes, and their metabolism and functions are regulated by the adjacent nucleate companion cells.

sentences.heading: Plant cell > Types of plant cells and tissues > Phloem
sentences.text: The companion cells, connected to the sieve tubes via plasmodesmata, are responsible for loading the phloem with sugars.

sentences.heading: Plant cell > Types of plant cells and tissues > Phloem
sentences.text: The bryophytes lack phloem, but moss sporophytes have a simpler tissue with analogous function known as the leptome.

sentences.heading: Plant cell > Types of plant cells and tissues > Epidermis
sentences.text: The plant epidermis is specialised tissue, composed of parenchyma cells, that covers the external surfaces of leaves, stems and roots.

sentences.heading: Plant cell > Types of plant cells and tissues > Epidermis
sentences.text: Several cell types may be present in the epidermis.

sentences.heading: Plant cell > Types of plant cells and tissues > Epidermis
sentences.text: Notable among these are the stomatal guard cells that control the rate of gas exchange between the plant and the atmosphere, glandular and clothing hairs or trichomes, and the root hairs of primary roots.

sentences.heading: Plant cell > Types of plant cells and tissues > Epidermis
sentences.text: In the shoot epidermis of most plants, only the guard cells have chloroplasts.

sentences.heading: Plant cell > Types of plant cells and tissues > Epidermis
sentences.text: Chloroplasts contain the green pigment chlorophyll which is needed for photosynthesis.

sentences.heading: Plant cell > Types of plant cells and tissues > Epidermis
sentences.text: The epidermal cells of aerial organs arise from the superficial layer of cells known as the tunica (L1 and L2 layers) that covers the plant shoot apex, whereas the cortex and vascular tissues arise from innermost layer of the shoot apex known as the corpus (L3 layer).

sentences.heading: Plant cell > Types of plant cells and tissues > Epidermis
sentences.text: The epidermis of roots originates from the layer of cells immediately beneath the root cap.

sentences.heading: Plant cell > Types of plant cells and tissues > Epidermis
sentences.text: The epidermis of all aerial organs, but not roots, is covered with a cuticle made of polyester cutin or polymer cutan (or both), with a superficial layer of epicuticular waxes.

sentences.heading: Plant cell > Types of plant cells and tissues > Epidermis
sentences.text: The epidermal cells of the primary shoot are thought to be the only plant cells with the biochemical capacity to synthesize cutin.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell
sentences.text: Red blood cells (RBCs), referred to as erythrocytes (from Ancient Greek erythros 'red' and kytos 'hollow vessel', with -cyte translated as 'cell' in modern usage) in academia and medical publishing, also known as red cells, erythroid cells, and rarely haematids, are the most common type of blood cell and the vertebrate's principal means of delivering oxygen (O2) to the body tissues—via blood flow through the circulatory system.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell
sentences.text: Erythrocytes take up oxygen in the lungs, or in fish the gills, and release it into tissues while squeezing through the body's capillaries.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell
sentences.text: The cytoplasm of a red blood cell is rich in hemoglobin (Hb), an iron-containing biomolecule that can bind oxygen.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell
sentences.text: It is responsible for the red color of the cells and the blood.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell
sentences.text: Each human red blood cell contains approximately 270 million hemoglobin molecules.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell
sentences.text: The cell membrane is composed of proteins and lipids, and this structure provides properties essential for physiological cell function such as deformability and stability of the blood cell while traversing the circulatory system and specifically the capillary network.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell
sentences.text: In humans, mature red blood cells are flexible biconcave disks.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell
sentences.text: They lack a cell nucleus (which is expelled during development) and organelles, to accommodate maximum space for hemoglobin; they can be viewed as sacks of hemoglobin, with a plasma membrane as the sack.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell
sentences.text: Approximately 2.4 million new erythrocytes are produced per second in human adults.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell
sentences.text: The cells develop in the bone marrow and circulate for about 100–120 days in the body before their components are recycled by macrophages.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell
sentences.text: Each circulation takes about 60 seconds (one minute).

sentences.heading: Red blood cell
sentences.text: Approximately 84% of the cells in the human body are the 20–30 trillion red blood cells.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell
sentences.text: Nearly half of the blood's volume (40% to 45%) is red blood cells.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell
sentences.text: Packed red blood cells are red blood cells that have been donated, processed, and stored in a blood bank for blood transfusion.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Structure > Vertebrates
sentences.text: The vast majority of vertebrates, including mammals and humans, have red blood cells.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Structure > Vertebrates
sentences.text: These erythrocytes are cells present in blood to transport oxygen.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Structure > Vertebrates
sentences.text: The only known vertebrates without red blood cells are the crocodile icefish (family Channichthyidae); they live in very oxygen-rich cold water and transport oxygen freely dissolved in their blood.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Structure > Vertebrates
sentences.text: While they no longer use hemoglobin, remnants of hemoglobin genes can be found in their genome.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Structure > Vertebrates
sentences.text: Vertebrate red blood cells consist mainly of hemoglobin, a complex metalloprotein containing heme groups whose iron atoms temporarily bind to oxygen molecules (O2) in the lungs or gills and release them throughout the body.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Structure > Vertebrates
sentences.text: Oxygen can easily diffuse through the erythrocyte's cell membrane.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Structure > Vertebrates
sentences.text: Hemoglobin in the red blood cells also carries some of the waste product carbon dioxide back from the tissues; most waste carbon dioxide, however, is transported back to the pulmonary capillaries of the lungs as bicarbonate (HCO3−) dissolved in the blood plasma.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Structure > Vertebrates
sentences.text: Myoglobin, a compound related to hemoglobin, acts to store oxygen in muscle cells.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Structure > Vertebrates
sentences.text: The color of red blood cells is due to the heme group of hemoglobin.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Structure > Vertebrates
sentences.text: The blood plasma alone is straw-colored, but the red blood cells change color depending on the state of the hemoglobin: when combined with oxygen the resulting oxyhemoglobin is scarlet, and when oxygen has been released the resulting deoxyhemoglobin is of a dark red burgundy color.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Structure > Vertebrates
sentences.text: However, blood can appear bluish when seen through the vessel wall and skin.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Structure > Vertebrates
sentences.text: Pulse oximetry takes advantage of the hemoglobin color change to directly measure the arterial blood oxygen saturation using colorimetric techniques.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Structure > Vertebrates
sentences.text: Hemoglobin also has a very high affinity for carbon monoxide, forming carboxyhemoglobin which is a very bright red in color.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Structure > Vertebrates
sentences.text: Flushed, confused patients with a saturation reading of 100% on pulse oximetry are sometimes found to be suffering from carbon monoxide poisoning.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Structure > Vertebrates
sentences.text: Having oxygen-carrying proteins inside specialized cells (as opposed to oxygen carriers being dissolved in body fluid) was an important step in the evolution of vertebrates as it allows for less viscous blood, higher concentrations of oxygen, and better diffusion of oxygen from the blood to the tissues.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Structure > Vertebrates
sentences.text: The size of red blood cells varies widely among vertebrate species; red blood cell width is on average about 25% larger than capillary diameter, and it has been hypothesized that this improves the oxygen transfer from red blood cells to tissues.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Structure > Mammals
sentences.text: The red blood cells of mammals are typically shaped as biconcave disks: flattened and depressed in the center, with a dumbbell-shaped cross section, and a torus-shaped rim on the edge of the disk.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Structure > Mammals
sentences.text: This shape allows for a high surface-area-to-volume (SA/V) ratio to facilitate diffusion of gases.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Structure > Mammals
sentences.text: However, there are some exceptions concerning shape in the artiodactyl order (even-toed ungulates including cattle, deer, and their relatives), which displays a wide variety of bizarre red blood cell morphologies: small and highly ovaloid cells in llamas and camels (family Camelidae), tiny spherical cells in mouse deer (family Tragulidae), and cells which assume fusiform, lanceolate, crescentic, and irregularly polygonal and other angular forms in red deer and wapiti (family Cervidae).

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Structure > Mammals
sentences.text: Members of this order have clearly evolved a mode of red blood cell development substantially different from the mammalian norm.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Structure > Mammals
sentences.text: Overall, mammalian red blood cells are remarkably flexible and deformable so as to squeeze through tiny capillaries, as well as to maximize their apposing surface by assuming a cigar shape, where they efficiently release their oxygen load.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Structure > Mammals
sentences.text: Red blood cells in mammals are unique amongst vertebrates as most species do not have nuclei when mature.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Structure > Mammals
sentences.text: They do have nuclei during early phases of erythropoiesis, but extrude them during development as they mature; this provides more space for hemoglobin.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Structure > Mammals
sentences.text: The red blood cells without nuclei, called reticulocytes, subsequently lose all other cellular organelles such as their mitochondria, Golgi apparatus and endoplasmic reticulum.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Structure > Mammals
sentences.text: The spleen acts as a reservoir of red blood cells, but this effect is somewhat limited in humans.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Structure > Mammals
sentences.text: In some other mammals such as dogs and horses, the spleen sequesters large numbers of red blood cells, which are dumped into the blood during times of exertion stress, yielding a higher oxygen transport capacity.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Structure > Human
sentences.text: A typical human red blood cell has a disk diameter of approximately 6.2–8.2 μm and a maximum thickness of 2–2.5 μm and a minimum thickness in the centre of 0.8–1 μm, being much smaller than most other human cells.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Structure > Human
sentences.text: These cells have an average volume of about 90 fL with a surface area of about 136 μm2, and can swell up to a sphere shape containing 150 fL, without membrane distension.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Structure > Human
sentences.text: Adult humans have roughly 20–30 trillion red blood cells at any given time, constituting approximately 70% of all cells by number.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Structure > Human
sentences.text: Women have about 4–5 million red blood cells per microliter (cubic millimeter) of blood and men about 5–6 million; people living at high altitudes with low oxygen tension will have more.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Structure > Human
sentences.text: Red blood cells are thus much more common than the other blood particles: there are about 4,000–11,000 white blood cells and about 150,000–400,000 platelets per microliter.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Structure > Human
sentences.text: Human red blood cells take on average 60 seconds to complete one cycle of circulation.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Structure > Human
sentences.text: The blood's red color is due to the spectral properties of the hemic iron ions in hemoglobin.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Structure > Human
sentences.text: Each hemoglobin molecule carries four heme groups; hemoglobin constitutes about a third of the total cell volume.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Structure > Human
sentences.text: Hemoglobin is responsible for the transport of more than 98% of the oxygen in the body (the remaining oxygen is carried dissolved in the blood plasma).

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Structure > Human
sentences.text: The red blood cells of an average adult human male store collectively about 2.5 grams of iron, representing about 65% of the total iron contained in the body.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Microstructure > Nucleus
sentences.text: Red blood cells in mammals are anucleate when mature, meaning that they lack a cell nucleus.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Microstructure > Nucleus
sentences.text: In comparison, the red blood cells of other vertebrates have nuclei; the only known exceptions are salamanders of the family Plethodontidae, where five different clades has evolved various degrees of enucleated red blood cells (most evolved in some species of the genus Batrachoseps), and fish of the genus Maurolicus.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Microstructure > Nucleus
sentences.text: The elimination of the nucleus in vertebrate red blood cells has been offered as an explanation for the subsequent accumulation of non-coding DNA in the genome.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Microstructure > Nucleus
sentences.text: The argument runs as follows: Efficient gas transport requires red blood cells to pass through very narrow capillaries, and this constrains their size.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Microstructure > Nucleus
sentences.text: In the absence of nuclear elimination, the accumulation of repeat sequences is constrained by the volume occupied by the nucleus, which increases with genome size.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Microstructure > Nucleus
sentences.text: Nucleated red blood cells in mammals consist of two forms: normoblasts, which are normal erythropoietic precursors to mature red blood cells, and megaloblasts, which are abnormally large precursors that occur in megaloblastic anemias.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Microstructure > Membrane composition
sentences.text: Red blood cells are deformable, flexible, are able to adhere to other cells, and are able to interface with immune cells.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Microstructure > Membrane composition
sentences.text: Their membrane plays many roles in this.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Microstructure > Membrane composition
sentences.text: These functions are highly dependent on the membrane composition.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Microstructure > Membrane composition
sentences.text: The red blood cell membrane is composed of 3 layers: the glycocalyx on the exterior, which is rich in carbohydrates; the lipid bilayer which contains many transmembrane proteins, besides its lipidic main constituents; and the membrane skeleton, a structural network of proteins located on the inner surface of the lipid bilayer.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Microstructure > Membrane composition
sentences.text: Half of the membrane mass in human and most mammalian red blood cells are proteins.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Microstructure > Membrane composition
sentences.text: The other half are lipids, namely phospholipids and cholesterol.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Microstructure > Membrane composition > Membrane lipids
sentences.text: The red blood cell membrane comprises a typical lipid bilayer, similar to what can be found in virtually all human cells.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Microstructure > Membrane composition > Membrane lipids
sentences.text: Simply put, this lipid bilayer is composed of cholesterol and phospholipids in equal proportions by weight.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Microstructure > Membrane composition > Membrane lipids
sentences.text: The lipid composition is important as it defines many physical properties such as membrane permeability and fluidity.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Microstructure > Membrane composition > Membrane lipids
sentences.text: Additionally, the activity of many membrane proteins is regulated by interactions with lipids in the bilayer.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Microstructure > Membrane composition > Membrane lipids
sentences.text: Unlike cholesterol, which is evenly distributed between the inner and outer leaflets, the 5 major phospholipids are asymmetrically disposed, as shown below:

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Microstructure > Membrane composition > Membrane lipids
sentences.text: This asymmetric phospholipid distribution among the bilayer is the result of the function of several energy-dependent and energy-independent phospholipid transport proteins.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Microstructure > Membrane composition > Membrane lipids
sentences.text: Proteins called "Flippases" move phospholipids from the outer to the inner monolayer, while others called "floppases" do the opposite operation, against a concentration gradient in an energy-dependent manner.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Microstructure > Membrane composition > Membrane lipids
sentences.text: Additionally, there are also "scramblase" proteins that move phospholipids in both directions at the same time, down their concentration gradients in an energy-independent manner.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Microstructure > Membrane composition > Membrane lipids
sentences.text: There is still considerable debate ongoing regarding the identity of these membrane maintenance proteins in the red cell membrane.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Microstructure > Membrane composition > Membrane lipids
sentences.text: The maintenance of an asymmetric phospholipid distribution in the bilayer (such as an exclusive localization of PS and PIs in the inner monolayer) is critical for the cell integrity and function due to several reasons:

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Microstructure > Membrane composition > Membrane lipids
sentences.text: The presence of specialized structures named "lipid rafts" in the red blood cell membrane have been described by recent studies.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Microstructure > Membrane composition > Membrane lipids
sentences.text: These are structures enriched in cholesterol and sphingolipids associated with specific membrane proteins, namely flotillins, STOMatins (band 7), G-proteins, and β-adrenergic receptors.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Microstructure > Membrane composition > Membrane lipids
sentences.text: Lipid rafts that have been implicated in cell signaling events in nonerythroid cells have been shown in erythroid cells to mediate β2-adregenic receptor signaling and increase cAMP levels, and thus regulating entry of malarial parasites into normal red cells.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Microstructure > Membrane composition > Membrane proteins
sentences.text: The proteins of the membrane skeleton are responsible for the deformability, flexibility and durability of the red blood cell, enabling it to squeeze through capillaries less than half the diameter of the red blood cell (7–8 μm) and recovering the discoid shape as soon as these cells stop receiving compressive forces, in a similar fashion to an object made of rubber.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Microstructure > Membrane composition > Membrane proteins
sentences.text: There are currently more than 50 known membrane proteins, which can exist in a few hundred up to a million copies per red blood cell.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Microstructure > Membrane composition > Membrane proteins
sentences.text: Approximately 25 of these membrane proteins carry the various blood group antigens, such as the A, B and Rh antigens, among many others.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Microstructure > Membrane composition > Membrane proteins
sentences.text: These membrane proteins can perform a wide diversity of functions, such as transporting ions and molecules across the red cell membrane, adhesion and interaction with other cells such as endothelial cells, as signaling receptors, as well as other currently unknown functions.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Microstructure > Membrane composition > Membrane proteins
sentences.text: The blood types of humans are due to variations in surface glycoproteins of red blood cells.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Microstructure > Membrane composition > Membrane proteins
sentences.text: Disorders of the proteins in these membranes are associated with many disorders, such as hereditary spherocytosis, hereditary elliptocytosis, hereditary stomatocytosis, and paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Microstructure > Membrane composition > Membrane proteins
sentences.text: The red blood cell membrane proteins organized according to their function:

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Microstructure > Membrane composition > Membrane proteins
sentences.text: Structural role – The following membrane proteins establish linkages with skeletal proteins and may play an important role in regulating cohesion between the lipid bilayer and membrane skeleton, likely enabling the red cell to maintain its favorable membrane surface area by preventing the membrane from collapsing (vesiculating).

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Microstructure > Surface electrostatic potential
sentences.text: The zeta potential is an electrochemical property of cell surfaces that is determined by the net electrical charge of molecules exposed at the surface of cell membranes of the cell.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Microstructure > Surface electrostatic potential
sentences.text: The normal zeta potential of the red blood cell is −15.7 millivolts (mV).

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Microstructure > Surface electrostatic potential
sentences.text: Much of this potential appears to be contributed by the exposed sialic acid residues in the membrane: their removal results in zeta potential of −6.06 mV.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Function > Role in CO2 transport
sentences.text: Recall that respiration, as illustrated schematically here with a unit of carbohydrate, produces about as many molecules of carbon dioxide, CO2, as it consumes of oxygen, O2.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Function > Role in CO2 transport
sentences.text: Thus, the function of the circulatory system is as much about the transport of carbon dioxide as about the transport of oxygen.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Function > Role in CO2 transport
sentences.text: As stated elsewhere in this article, most of the carbon dioxide in the blood is in the form of bicarbonate ion.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Function > Role in CO2 transport
sentences.text: The bicarbonate provides a critical pH buffer.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Function > Role in CO2 transport
sentences.text: Thus, unlike hemoglobin for O2 transport, there is a physiological advantage to not having a specific CO2 transporter molecule.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Function > Role in CO2 transport
sentences.text: Red blood cells, nevertheless, play a key role in the CO2 transport process, for two reasons.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Function > Role in CO2 transport
sentences.text: First, because, besides hemoglobin, they contain a large number of copies of the enzyme carbonic anhydrase on the inside of their cell membrane.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Function > Role in CO2 transport
sentences.text: Carbonic anhydrase, as its name suggests, acts as a catalyst of the exchange between carbonic acid and carbon dioxide (which is the anhydride of carbonic acid).

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Function > Role in CO2 transport
sentences.text: Because it is a catalyst, it can affect many CO2 molecules, so it performs its essential role without needing as many copies as are needed for O2 transport by hemoglobin.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Function > Role in CO2 transport
sentences.text: In the presence of this catalyst carbon dioxide and carbonic acid reach an equilibrium very rapidly, while the red cells are still moving through the capillary.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Function > Role in CO2 transport
sentences.text: Thus it is the RBC that ensures that most of the CO2 is transported as bicarbonate.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Function > Role in CO2 transport
sentences.text: At physiological pH the equilibrium strongly favors carbonic acid, which is mostly dissociated into bicarbonate ion.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Function > Role in CO2 transport
sentences.text: The H+ ions released by this rapid reaction within RBC, while still in the capillary, act to reduce the oxygen binding affinity of hemoglobin, the Bohr effect.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Function > Role in CO2 transport
sentences.text: The second major contribution of RBC to carbon dioxide transport is that carbon dioxide directly reacts with globin protein components of hemoglobin to form carbaminohemoglobin compounds.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Function > Role in CO2 transport
sentences.text: As oxygen is released in the tissues, more CO2 binds to hemoglobin, and as oxygen binds in the lung, it displaces the hemoglobin bound CO2, this is called the Haldane effect.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Function > Role in CO2 transport
sentences.text: Despite the fact that only a small amount of the CO2 in blood is bound to hemoglobin in venous blood, a greater proportion of the change in CO2 content between venous and arterial blood comes from the change in this bound CO2.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Function > Role in CO2 transport
sentences.text: That is, there is always an abundance of bicarbonate in blood, both venous and arterial, because of its aforementioned role as a pH buffer.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Function > Role in CO2 transport
sentences.text: In summary, carbon dioxide produced by cellular respiration diffuses very rapidly to areas of lower concentration, specifically into nearby capillaries.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Function > Role in CO2 transport
sentences.text: When it diffuses into a RBC, CO2 is rapidly converted by the carbonic anhydrase found on the inside of the RBC membrane into bicarbonate ion.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Function > Role in CO2 transport
sentences.text: The bicarbonate ions in turn leave the RBC in exchange for chloride ions from the plasma, facilitated by the band 3 anion transport protein colocated in the RBC membrane.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Function > Role in CO2 transport
sentences.text: The bicarbonate ion does not diffuse back out of the capillary, but is carried to the lung.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Function > Role in CO2 transport
sentences.text: In the lung the lower partial pressure of carbon dioxide in the alveoli causes carbon dioxide to diffuse rapidly from the capillary into the alveoli.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Function > Role in CO2 transport
sentences.text: The carbonic anhydrase in the red cells keeps the bicarbonate ion in equilibrium with carbon dioxide.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Function > Role in CO2 transport
sentences.text: So as carbon dioxide leaves the capillary, and CO2 is displaced by O2 on hemoglobin, sufficient bicarbonate ion converts rapidly to carbon dioxide to maintain the equilibrium.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Function > Secondary functions
sentences.text: When red blood cells undergo shear stress in constricted vessels, they release ATP, which causes the vessel walls to relax and dilate so as to promote normal blood flow.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Function > Secondary functions
sentences.text: When their hemoglobin molecules are deoxygenated, red blood cells release S-Nitrosothiols, which also act to dilate blood vessels, thus directing more blood to areas of the body depleted of oxygen.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Function > Secondary functions
sentences.text: Red blood cells can also synthesize nitric oxide enzymatically, using L-arginine as substrate, as do endothelial cells.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Function > Secondary functions
sentences.text: Exposure of red blood cells to physiological levels of shear stress activates nitric oxide synthase and export of nitric oxide, which may contribute to the regulation of vascular tonus.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Function > Secondary functions
sentences.text: Red blood cells can also produce hydrogen sulfide, a signalling gas that acts to relax vessel walls.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Function > Secondary functions
sentences.text: It is believed that the cardioprotective effects of garlic are due to red blood cells converting its sulfur compounds into hydrogen sulfide.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Function > Secondary functions
sentences.text: Red blood cells also play a part in the body's immune response: when lysed by pathogens such as bacteria, their hemoglobin releases free radicals, which break down the pathogen's cell wall and membrane, killing it.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Function > Cellular processes
sentences.text: As a result of not containing mitochondria, red blood cells use none of the oxygen they transport; instead they produce the energy carrier ATP by the glycolysis of glucose and lactic acid fermentation on the resulting pyruvate.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Function > Cellular processes
sentences.text: Furthermore, the pentose phosphate pathway plays an important role in red blood cells; see glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency for more information.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Function > Cellular processes
sentences.text: As red blood cells contain no nucleus, protein biosynthesis is currently assumed to be absent in these cells.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Function > Cellular processes
sentences.text: Because of the lack of nuclei and organelles, mature red blood cells do not contain DNA and cannot synthesize any RNA (although it does contain RNAs), and consequently cannot divide and have limited repair capabilities.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Function > Cellular processes
sentences.text: The inability to carry out protein synthesis means that no virus can evolve to target mammalian red blood cells.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Function > Cellular processes
sentences.text: However, infection with parvoviruses (such as human parvovirus B19) can affect erythroid precursors while they still have DNA, as recognized by the presence of giant pronormoblasts with viral particles and inclusion bodies, thus temporarily depleting the blood of reticulocytes and causing anemia.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Life cycle
sentences.text: Human red blood cells are produced through a process named erythropoiesis, developing from committed stem cells to mature red blood cells in about 7 days.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Life cycle
sentences.text: When matured, in a healthy individual these cells live in blood circulation for about 100 to 120 days (and 80 to 90 days in a full term infant).

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Life cycle
sentences.text: At the end of their lifespan, they are removed from circulation.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Life cycle
sentences.text: In many chronic diseases, the lifespan of the red blood cells is reduced.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Life cycle > Creation
sentences.text: Erythropoiesis is the process by which new red blood cells are produced; it lasts about 7 days.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Life cycle > Creation
sentences.text: Through this process red blood cells are continuously produced in the red bone marrow of large bones.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Life cycle > Creation
sentences.text: (In the embryo, the liver is the main site of red blood cell production.)

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Life cycle > Creation
sentences.text: The production can be stimulated by the hormone erythropoietin (EPO), synthesised by the kidney.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Life cycle > Creation
sentences.text: Just before and after leaving the bone marrow, the developing cells are known as reticulocytes; these constitute about 1% of circulating red blood cells.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Life cycle > Functional lifetime
sentences.text: The functional lifetime of a red blood cell is about 100–120 days, during which time the red blood cells are continually moving in the circulatory system.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Life cycle > Senescence
sentences.text: The aging red blood cell undergoes changes in its plasma membrane, making it susceptible to selective recognition by macrophages and subsequent phagocytosis in the mononuclear phagocyte system (spleen, liver and lymph nodes), thus removing old and defective cells and continually purging the blood.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Life cycle > Senescence
sentences.text: This process is termed eryptosis, red blood cell programmed death.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Life cycle > Senescence
sentences.text: This process normally occurs at the same rate of production by erythropoiesis, balancing the total circulating red blood cell count.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Life cycle > Senescence
sentences.text: Eryptosis is increased in a wide variety of diseases including sepsis, haemolytic uremic syndrome, malaria, sickle cell anemia, beta-thalassemia, glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, phosphate depletion, iron deficiency and Wilson's disease.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Life cycle > Senescence
sentences.text: Eryptosis can be elicited by osmotic shock, oxidative stress, and energy depletion, as well as by a wide variety of endogenous mediators and xenobiotics.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Life cycle > Senescence
sentences.text: Excessive eryptosis is observed in red blood cells lacking the cGMP-dependent protein kinase type I or the AMP-activated protein kinase AMPK.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Life cycle > Senescence
sentences.text: Inhibitors of eryptosis include erythropoietin, nitric oxide, catecholamines and high concentrations of urea.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Life cycle > Senescence
sentences.text: Much of the resulting breakdown products are recirculated in the body.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Life cycle > Senescence
sentences.text: The heme constituent of hemoglobin are broken down into iron (Fe3+) and biliverdin.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Life cycle > Senescence
sentences.text: The biliverdin is reduced to bilirubin, which is released into the plasma and recirculated to the liver bound to albumin.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Life cycle > Senescence
sentences.text: The iron is released into the plasma to be recirculated by a carrier protein called transferrin.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Life cycle > Senescence
sentences.text: Almost all red blood cells are removed in this manner from the circulation before they are old enough to hemolyze.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Life cycle > Senescence
sentences.text: Hemolyzed hemoglobin is bound to a protein in plasma called haptoglobin, which is not excreted by the kidney.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Clinical significance > Disease
sentences.text: Blood diseases involving the red blood cells include:

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Clinical significance > Transfusion
sentences.text: Red blood cells may be given as part of a blood transfusion.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Clinical significance > Transfusion
sentences.text: Blood may be donated from another person, or stored by the recipient at an earlier date.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Clinical significance > Transfusion
sentences.text: Donated blood usually requires screening to ensure that donors do not contain risk factors for the presence of blood-borne diseases, or will not suffer themselves by giving blood.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Clinical significance > Transfusion
sentences.text: Blood is usually collected and tested for common or serious blood-borne diseases including Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C and HIV.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Clinical significance > Transfusion
sentences.text: The blood type (A, B, AB, or O) or the blood product is identified and matched with the recipient's blood to minimise the likelihood of acute hemolytic transfusion reaction, a type of transfusion reaction.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Clinical significance > Transfusion
sentences.text: This relates to the presence of antigens on the cell's surface.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Clinical significance > Transfusion
sentences.text: After this process, the blood is stored, and within a short duration is used.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Clinical significance > Transfusion
sentences.text: Blood can be given as a whole product or the red blood cells separated as packed red blood cells.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Clinical significance > Transfusion
sentences.text: Blood is often transfused when there is known anaemia, active bleeding, or when there is an expectation of serious blood loss, such as prior to an operation.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Clinical significance > Transfusion
sentences.text: Before blood is given, a small sample of the recipient's blood is tested with the transfusion in a process known as cross-matching.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Clinical significance > Transfusion
sentences.text: In 2008 it was reported that human embryonic stem cells had been successfully coaxed into becoming red blood cells in the lab.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Clinical significance > Transfusion
sentences.text: The difficult step was to induce the cells to eject their nucleus; this was achieved by growing the cells on stromal cells from the bone marrow.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Clinical significance > Transfusion
sentences.text: It is hoped that these artificial red blood cells can eventually be used for blood transfusions.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Clinical significance > Transfusion
sentences.text: A human trial is conducted in 2022, using blood cultured from stem cells obtained from donor blood.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Clinical significance > Tests
sentences.text: Several blood tests involve red blood cells.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Clinical significance > Tests
sentences.text: These include a RBC count (the number of red blood cells per volume of blood), calculation of the hematocrit (percentage of blood volume occupied by red blood cells), and the erythrocyte sedimentation rate.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Clinical significance > Tests
sentences.text: The blood type needs to be determined to prepare for a blood transfusion or an organ transplantation.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Clinical significance > Tests
sentences.text: Many diseases involving red blood cells are diagnosed with a blood film (or peripheral blood smear), where a thin layer of blood is smeared on a microscope slide.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Clinical significance > Tests
sentences.text: This may reveal poikilocytosis, which are variations in red blood cell shape.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Clinical significance > Tests
sentences.text: When red blood cells sometimes occur as a stack, flat side next to flat side.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Clinical significance > Tests
sentences.text: This is known as rouleaux formation, and it occurs more often if the levels of certain serum proteins are elevated, as for instance during inflammation.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Clinical significance > Separation and blood doping
sentences.text: Red blood cells can be obtained from whole blood by centrifugation, which separates the cells from the blood plasma in a process known as blood fractionation.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Clinical significance > Separation and blood doping
sentences.text: Packed red blood cells, which are made in this way from whole blood with the plasma removed, are used in transfusion medicine.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Clinical significance > Separation and blood doping
sentences.text: During plasma donation, the red blood cells are pumped back into the body right away and only the plasma is collected.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Clinical significance > Separation and blood doping
sentences.text: Some athletes have tried to improve their performance by blood doping: first about 1 litre of their blood is extracted, then the red blood cells are isolated, frozen and stored, to be reinjected shortly before the competition.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Clinical significance > Separation and blood doping
sentences.text: (Red blood cells can be conserved for 5 weeks at −79 °C or −110 °F, or over 10 years using cryoprotectants) This practice is hard to detect but may endanger the human cardiovascular system which is not equipped to deal with blood of the resulting higher viscosity.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Clinical significance > Separation and blood doping
sentences.text: Another method of blood doping involves injection with erythropoietin to stimulate production of red blood cells.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > Clinical significance > Separation and blood doping

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > History
sentences.text: The first person to describe red blood cells was the young Dutch biologist Jan Swammerdam, who had used an early microscope in 1658 to study the blood of a frog.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > History
sentences.text: Unaware of this work, Anton van Leeuwenhoek provided another microscopic description in 1674, this time providing a more precise description of red blood cells, even approximating their size, "25,000 times smaller than a fine grain of sand".

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > History
sentences.text: In the 1740s, Vincenzo Menghini in Bologna was able to demonstrate the presence of iron by passing magnets over the powder or ash remaining from heated red blood cells.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > History
sentences.text: In 1901, Karl Landsteiner published his discovery of the three main blood groups—A, B, and C (which he later renamed to O).

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > History
sentences.text: Landsteiner described the regular patterns in which reactions occurred when serum was mixed with red blood cells, thus identifying compatible and conflicting combinations between these blood groups.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > History
sentences.text: A year later Alfred von Decastello and Adriano Sturli, two colleagues of Landsteiner, identified a fourth blood group—AB.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > History
sentences.text: In 1959, by use of X-ray crystallography, Max Perutz was able to unravel the structure of hemoglobin, the red blood cell protein that carries oxygen.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > History
sentences.text: The oldest intact red blood cells ever discovered were found in Ötzi the Iceman, a natural mummy of a man who died around 3255 BCE.

sentences.heading: Red blood cell > History
sentences.text: These cells were discovered in May 2012.

sentences.heading: Root hair
sentences.text: Root hairs or absorbent hairs, are outgrowths of epidermal cells, specialized cells at the tip of a plant root.

sentences.heading: Root hair
sentences.text: They are lateral extensions of a single cell and are only rarely branched.

sentences.heading: Root hair
sentences.text: They are found in the region of maturation, of the root.

sentences.heading: Root hair
sentences.text: Root hair cells improve plant water absorption by increasing root surface area to volume ratio which allows the root hair cell to take in more water.

sentences.heading: Root hair
sentences.text: The large vacuole inside root hair cells makes this intake much more efficient.

sentences.heading: Root hair
sentences.text: Root hairs are also important for nutrient uptake as they are main interface between plants and mycorrhizal fungi.

sentences.heading: Root hair > Function
sentences.text: The function of all root hairs is to collect water and mineral nutrients in the soil to be sent throughout the plant.

sentences.heading: Root hair > Function
sentences.text: In roots, most water absorption happens through the root hairs.

sentences.heading: Root hair > Function
sentences.text: The length of root hairs allows them to penetrate between soil particles and prevents harmful bacterial organisms from entering the plant through the xylem vessels.

sentences.heading: Root hair > Function
sentences.text: Increasing the surface area of these hairs makes plants more efficient in absorbing nutrients and interacting with microbes.

sentences.heading: Root hair > Function
sentences.text: As root hair cells do not carry out photosynthesis, they do not contain chloroplasts.

sentences.heading: Root hair > Importance
sentences.text: Root hairs form an important surface as they are needed to absorb most of the water and nutrients needed for the plant.

sentences.heading: Root hair > Importance
sentences.text: They are also directly involved in the formation of root nodules in legume plants.

sentences.heading: Root hair > Importance
sentences.text: The root hairs curl around the bacteria, which allows for the formation of an infection thread into the dividing cortical cells to form the nodule.

sentences.heading: Root hair > Importance
sentences.text: Having a large surface area, the active uptake of water and minerals through root hairs is highly efficient.

sentences.heading: Root hair > Importance
sentences.text: Root hair cells also secrete acids (e.g., malic and citric acid), which solubilize minerals by changing their oxidation state, making the ions easier to absorb.

sentences.heading: Root hair > Formation
sentences.text: Root hair cells vary between 15 and 17 micrometers in diameter, and 80 and 1,500 micrometers in length.

sentences.heading: Root hair > Formation
sentences.text: Root hairs are found only in the zone of maturation, also called the zone of differentiation.

sentences.heading: Root hair > Formation
sentences.text: They are not found in the zone of elongation, possibly because older root hairs are sheared off as the root elongates and moves through the soil.

sentences.heading: Root hair > Formation
sentences.text: Root hairs grow quickly, at least 1 μm/min, making them particularly useful for research on cell expansion.

sentences.heading: Root hair > Formation
sentences.text: Just prior to and during root hair cell development, there is elevated phosphorylase activity.

sentences.heading: Root hair > Fungal interaction
sentences.text: Root hairs are essential for healthy plant nutrition, especially through their interactions with symbiotic fungi.

sentences.heading: Root hair > Fungal interaction
sentences.text: Symbiotic fungi and root hairs produce mycorrhizal symbioses like arbuscular mycorrhiza, formed by AM fungi, and ectomycorrhiza, formed by EM fungi.

sentences.heading: Root hair > Fungal interaction
sentences.text: These are very common, occurring in 90% of terrestrial plant species, because of the benefits it brings to both the fungus and plant.

sentences.heading: Root hair > Fungal interaction
sentences.text: Formation of this relationship for EM fungi begins with the colonization of the root hairs.

sentences.heading: Root hair > Fungal interaction
sentences.text: This process begins when the EM fungus adheres to the root hair from the soil.

sentences.heading: Root hair > Fungal interaction
sentences.text: The fungus then secretes diffusible factors, to which root hairs are highly sensitive, allowing the hyphae to penetrate into the epidermal cells and create a Hartig net in the first layers of the root cortex.

sentences.heading: Root hair > Fungal interaction
sentences.text: This highly branched structure serves as an interface between the two organisms as fungal cells adapt to the exchanges that occur between the plant and fungus.

sentences.heading: Root hair > Fungal interaction
sentences.text: This process is similar to how AM fungi colonize root hairs, but instead of diffusible factors, they secrete hydrolases to relax the cell wall, which allows hyphae to enter, and there is no Hartig net.

sentences.heading: Root hair > Fungal interaction
sentences.text: Various effects of fungal colonization in root hairs show that this relationship is beneficial to both plant and fungal species, but the main effect is on root hair growth.

sentences.heading: Root hair > Fungal interaction
sentences.text: Fungi actually affect the growth of root hairs if there is water or nutrient deficiency.

sentences.heading: Root hair > Fungal interaction
sentences.text: Since both of these organisms require nutrients and water, their cooperation is essential to their mutual survival.

sentences.heading: Root hair > Fungal interaction
sentences.text: Upon detection of deficiency, the drought stress response of the plant is triggered, causing growth of the root hairs.

sentences.heading: Root hair > Fungal interaction
sentences.text: The mycorrhizae of the fungus then uses its extended system to help the plant find the correct area of nutrition, signaling the direction in which the roots should grow.

sentences.heading: Root hair > Fungal interaction
sentences.text: This makes root growth more efficient, preserving energy for other metabolic processes, which in turn benefits the fungus that feeds off those metabolic products.

sentences.heading: Root hair > Survival
sentences.text: When a new root hair cell grows, it excretes a hormone that inhibits the growth of root hairs in nearby cells.

sentences.heading: Root hair > Survival
sentences.text: This ensures equal and efficient distribution of the actual hairs on these cells.

sentences.heading: Root hair > Survival
sentences.text: Repotting or transplanting a plant can result in root hair cells being pulled off, perhaps to a significant extent, which can cause wilting.

sections.outcome: Describe the parts a plant cell has that an animal cell does not, and what they do

keyIdeas.statement: A plant cell has a cell wall outside its cell membrane, unlike an animal cell.
keyIdeas.explanation: The wall contains cellulose and helps the plant cell keep its shape, helping to support plant tissues and organs.

keyIdeas.statement: A red blood cell is adapted to carry oxygen around the body.
keyIdeas.explanation: It contains haemoglobin, which binds oxygen. Its flexible, biconcave shape helps it exchange gases and pass through tiny capillaries.
keyIdeas.example: A mature human red blood cell has no nucleus, leaving more room for haemoglobin.

keyIdeas.statement: A root hair cell is adapted to absorb water and mineral nutrients from the soil.
keyIdeas.explanation: Its long extension gives it a large surface area compared with its volume, so absorption is more efficient. A large vacuole also makes water intake more effective.
keyIdeas.example: Root hairs can extend between soil particles, where they collect water and minerals for the plant.
